claims.text: Adding Mo to TiVNbTa will improve its elevated-temperature mechanical properties.
Mo-modified TiVNbTa will retain the thermal conductivity needed for effective W-to-CuCrZr heat transfer.
Baseline TiVNbTa is a single-phase BCC dendritic alloy.
Baseline TiVNbTa has a room-temperature yield strength of approximately 800 MPa.
Baseline TiVNbTa has yield and compressive strengths of 330 MPa and 423 MPa, respectively, at 1273 K and approximately 30% strain.
The intervention is to add a modest, controlled amount of Mo during TiVNbTa synthesis.
The Mo-modified alloy will retain a single-phase BCC structure.
Mo addition will enhance solid-solution strengthening in TiVNbTa.
Mo addition will promote edge-dislocation-mediated deformation at high temperature.
MoNbTaW and MoNbTaVW retain high strength at temperatures above 1200 °C.
Mo-induced solid-solution strengthening and edge-dislocation slip will retard temperature-dependent softening in TiVNbTa.
Mo-modified TiVNbTa will have a yield strength greater than 330 MPa at 1273 K.
Mo-modified TiVNbTa will have greater compressive strength than baseline TiVNbTa at 1273 K.
The modified intermediate layer will continue to transfer heat efficiently between W and CuCrZr.
Testing at approximately 1273 K and up to 30% strain represents the relevant operating boundaries for both the W component and CuCrZr heat sink.
High-temperature strength retention and sufficient thermal conductivity are both critical for the intermediate layer.
The magnitude of the strength improvement depends on Mo content and processing conditions and is not yet known.
A controlled comparison at 1273 K can test whether Mo-modified TiVNbTa has statistically higher yield and compressive strengths than baseline TiVNbTa.
XRD and TEM can test BCC phase retention and the proposed dislocation structure, while thermal-conductivity measurements can test heat-transfer retention.

contradictions.description: The conditions field says testing near 1273 K matches the operating limits of both W and CuCrZr, whereas the boundary field describes CuCrZr as restricted to a lower-temperature operating range. No temperature gradient or interface-specific CuCrZr temperature is specified to reconcile these statements.
